limits: Describes nonpositional, docID-ordered inverted indexes for keyword (Boolean/tf-idf) retrieval; no dense vector, ANN (HNSW, IVF, PQ) or embedding index construction.
Hardware parameters are 2007 (5 ms seek, spinning disk, several GB RAM, 1 TB disk); SSDs, NVMe, and RAM of hundreds of GB change the BSBI/SPIMI trade-offs.
MapReduce and Hadoop (cited at lucene.apache.org/hadoop) are dated; Spark and managed search services have replaced them.
No experiments: the only data is Reuters-RCV1 statistics (Table 4.2) used in worked examples; Table 4.3 time column is left as Exercise 4.6.
Compression is deferred to Chapter 5; ranked retrieval details to Chapters 6-7; security of ACLs only sketched.
Authors concede multiple-index schemes complicate collection statistics such as idf and spelling correction, p.80.
practices: Keep frequently used disk data in memory (caching) and store data read together contiguously to cut seeks, p.68.
Store compressed data on disk: read plus decompress is usually faster than reading uncompressed, p.69.
For collections too large for memory use blocked sort-based indexing: parse blocks that fit memory, invert, write, merge with a priority queue, p.71.
Prefer SPIMI when the term-to-termID map does not fit in memory: per-block dictionaries, postings lists that double in size, sort terms before writing, p.73-74.
For web-scale collections use MapReduce with parsers and inverters; split input into 16 or 64 MB chunks reassigned on failure, p.75.
For a static or slowly changing collection rebuild the index periodically while the old one serves queries, p.78.
For quick freshness keep a small in-memory auxiliary index plus an invalidation bit vector for deletions, and merge when it grows, p.78.
Use logarithmic merging to lower update cost, accepting slower queries across log(T/n) indexes, p.79-80.
Order postings by impact for ranked retrieval to allow early termination; docID order for compression, p.81.
Enforce document-level security via ACL inverted lists intersected with results, or check the file system at query time, p.81.

terms.definition: the process of constructing an inverted index; the process or machine that performs it
time to position the disk head in a new position; averages 5 ms for typical disks
blocked sort-based indexing: segments the collection into equal parts, sorts termID-docID pairs of each in memory, stores sorted runs on disk, merges them
single-pass in-memory indexing: uses terms instead of termIDs, writes each block's dictionary to disk, then starts a new dictionary
a general architecture for distributed computing designed for large computer clusters of commodity machines
machines executing the map phase / the reduce phase that collects all docIDs for a termID into a postings list
a small in-memory index storing new documents, searched together with the large main index
maintain indexes I0, I1, ... of size 2^i x n so each posting is merged once per level
representation of each document as the set of users that can access it; inverted to a per-user access list
